triple-agonist.definition: One drug molecule that switches on three different receptors. Retatrutide switches on the receptors for GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon.

agonist.definition: A substance that fits a receptor and switches it on, in the same way as the body's own messenger.

glucagon-receptor.definition: The receptor that the hormone glucagon switches on. It is found mainly in the liver, where it tells cells to release sugar and use fat and amino acids.

glp-1-receptor.definition: The receptor that the gut hormone GLP-1 switches on. It is found in the pancreas, the brain, the gut and the heart.

energy-expenditure.definition: The amount of energy the body uses in a day: for keeping warm, breathing, digesting food and moving.

dysaesthesia.definition: An unpleasant, abnormal feeling in the skin, such as burning, tingling or soreness, without an obvious cause.

allodynia.definition: Pain from something that does not normally hurt, such as clothes touching the skin.

hyperaesthesia.definition: Skin that is more sensitive than normal to touch, heat or cold.

investigational-medicine.definition: A medicine that is still being tested in clinical trials and has no marketing authorisation. In the US, the UK, Canada and Australia it may be supplied only through narrow exceptions, mainly authorised trials and formal access routes.

expanded-access.definition: In the US, a legal route in which a doctor asks the company, under the FDA's rules, for an unapproved medicine for a seriously ill patient who cannot join a trial.

biologics-license-application.definition: The formal request a company sends to the US FDA to approve a biological medicine. The FDA then reviews the data before it decides.

topline-results.definition: The first headline numbers from a trial, released by the company before independent experts have checked the full results.

peer-review.definition: Checking of a study by independent experts before a journal publishes it. It catches some errors, but it does not prove that the results are right.

dxa-scan.definition: A low-dose X-ray scan that measures how much of the body is fat, lean tissue and bone.

masld.definition: Too much fat stored in the liver, linked to overweight, diabetes and high blood fats. Over years it can lead to liver inflammation and scarring.

ketones.definition: Acids that the liver makes from fat when the body has too little sugar or too little insulin. Small amounts are normal; very high amounts make the blood acidic.

diabetic-ketoacidosis.definition: A dangerous condition in which a lack of insulin lets ketones build up and make the blood acidic. It needs emergency treatment.

arrhythmia.definition: A heartbeat that is too fast, too slow or irregular.

atrial-fibrillation.definition: A common irregular heartbeat in which the upper chambers of the heart quiver instead of beating in rhythm. It raises the risk of stroke.

tachycardia.definition: A heart rate at rest that is faster than normal, usually more than 100 beats a minute in adults.

palpitations.definition: Feeling your own heartbeat as pounding, racing, fluttering or skipping.

sinoatrial-node.definition: A small group of cells in the right upper chamber of the heart. It works as the heart's natural pacemaker and sets the heart rate.

inotropic-effect.definition: A change in how strongly heart muscle squeezes. A positive inotropic effect makes it squeeze harder.

cryo-em.definition: A method that freezes molecules and images them with electrons, to show their three-dimensional shape in fine detail.

hypotension.definition: Blood pressure that is lower than normal. It can cause dizziness or fainting, especially when standing up.

post-hoc-analysis.definition: An analysis that researchers chose after the data were collected. It can suggest ideas, but it is weaker evidence than an analysis planned in advance.

substudy.definition: A smaller study inside a larger trial, with extra tests in some of the trial's participants.

network-meta-analysis.definition: A method that combines many trials to compare treatments, including treatments never tested against each other directly. Such indirect comparisons are less certain than head-to-head trials.

case-report.definition: A published description of what happened to one patient. It can raise an alarm, but it cannot show what caused the problem.

mass-spectrometry.definition: A laboratory method that identifies molecules by weighing them very precisely. Anti-doping laboratories use it to find drugs in blood and urine.

angptl3-8.definition: A pair of proteins made by the liver that slows the breakdown of fats in the blood. Lower levels go with lower triglycerides.

clinical-trial-phases.definition: The steps of testing a new medicine in people. Phase 1 checks safety in a few dozen people, phase 2 tests doses in hundreds, and phase 3 confirms benefits and harms in thousands.

international-nonproprietary-name.definition: The official generic name of a medicine, chosen through the World Health Organization, such as retatrutide or semaglutide.

pharmacovigilance.definition: Watching for and studying the side effects of medicines once people use them, for example through reports from patients and doctors.
